DECEMBER 16, 1972, BILLBOARD 
HELSINKI-The appearance of 
a new Finnish company specializ- 
ing in record and cassette imports 
has caused surprise in the industry 
here, and renewed concern about 
illegal importation, hitherto strict- 
ly controlled by the Finnish branch 
of the International Federation of 
Phonographic Industries and 
TEOSTO, the Finnish composers 
copyright bureau. 
Local recording companies are 
studying an advertisement which 
appeared at full length in a Fin- 
nish pop consumer magazine. It 
stated that a Tampere -based com- 
pany is importing all product direct 
from the U.S.A., Britain, France 
and Spain, including labels already 
represented and licensed in Fin- 
land. The company claims it can 
offer "hot product" well before it 
becomes available from the usual 
outlets, and that because of its 
overseas agreements it can sell all 
standard priced cassettes ($6.70) 
with 30 percent discount. 
Finnish re co r d manufacturers 
admit that investing and keeping 
track of such an operation is labo- 
rious. Usually independent import- 
ers deal with big American ex- 
porters, who are offering cut-off 
and 
discount 
material. 
Though 
this latter has minimal appeal in 
the States, it is selling well in Fin- 
nish supermarkets and similar out- 
lets, but represents only a minor 
irritation for the local disk com- 
panies. "Hot product" hit importa- 
tions exert a more serious effect, 
as has been noted in Britain, West 
Germany and Sweden. 
A music 
industry spokesman 
stated that all suspected cases of 
illegal importing are investigated, 
and if necessary, referred to legal 
authorities and TEOSTO, which 
is involved with mechanical copy- 
rights and performing rights.

. As part of its efforts to

the U.K., the National Council for 
Cancer Research has arranged with 
RCA for the release on an album, 
the proceeds of which will be do- 
nated to the clinics. The album, 
"Close to You," includes tracks 
by Jack Jones, Perry Como, Ray- 
mond Lefevre, Henry Mancini and 
the Glenn Miller Band. The artists 
and the executors of the Miller es- 
tate have agreed to donate all their 
royalties to the fund. It is under- 
stood that the National Council 
for Cancer Research re q u i r es 
around $2,400,000 to build the 
clinics. 
Cliff Richard, who has been pro- 
duced for EMI's Columbia label 
by Norrie Paramor since his first 
record "Move It" in 1959, has be- 
gun to use other producers. Peter 
Gormley, Cliff Richard's manager, 
told Billboard, that the singer 
wanted to experiment with new 
producers and that Paramor would 
continue to be involved in certain 
projects. He stressed that Richard 
and Paramor had not parted com- 
pany. Cliff Richard's latest single 
in the U.K., "Brand New Song," 
was co -produced by Paramor with 
New Seekers producer Dave Mc- 
Kay. Norrie Paramor has now 
been appointed the principal con- 
ductor of the Midland Light or- 
chestra and told Billboard that this 
position would eventually take up 
a great deal of his time. 
United Artists is issuing an al- 
bum, "The Golden Age of the 
Hollywood Musical," featuring mu- 
sic from the spectacular dance se- 
quences staged by Busby Berkeley 
in films between 1932 and 1935. 
A release for the album is also 
scheduled for America. The album, 
which has been in the planning for 
two years, was conceived by Alan 
Warner of UA. "The Golden Age 
of the Hollywood Musical" in- 
cludes music from "42nd Street," 
"Dames" and "Footlight Parade." 
Singer -writer Neil Sedaka was 
in London recently to promote his 
"Oh Carol" record in the U.K. 
Sedaka also promoted his new rec- 
ord "Beautiful You" on RCA... .

February beginning in Germany.

Dear FIND Dealers: 
"We've been able to get records 
we never could before through 
using FIND," says Frances Nel- 
son, assistant manager of Sybel's 
Golden 
Oldie 
Records 
in 
Fort 
Worth. The FIND catalog is par- 
ticularly 
helpful, 
according to 
Ms. Nelson. "Records are listed 
by category, which is one major 
help," she says. "Also, the price 
is next to each item so the con- 
sumer knows up front what he 
or she will have to pay. Because 
of this, we find many customers 
paying in advance. The catalog 
on the whole is very informative. 
"Oldies are big with us, as wall 
as 
contemporary 
music," 
she 
adds, "and this is where we get 
a lot of help from FIND. Older 
soundtracks are easy for us to 
get, and so are records by big 
bands and artists such ;s Hank 
Williams, Judy Garland and Al 
Jolson. This helps us take advan- 
tage of the nostalgia 
craze at 
the moment 
as well 
as 
help 
people who naturally 
have an 
interest in these LP's." 
The outlet advertises special or- 
ders and mentions FIND in the 
ads. The catalog is displayed on 
the counter, with sales personnel 
doing the actual order taking. 
"We know we're getting 
a 
re- 
peat business because of FIND." 
Ms. Nelson adds. 
'We tell our 
customers that if we don't see 
the 
record they want 
in 
the 
FIND catalog, it's not available. 
So far, it's all worked out very 
well, 
including reasonable 
de- 
livery time and the knowledge 
that 
we 
can 
get 
records 
we 
never could get before." 
Dealer response to the new FIND 
catalog 
has been 
good so far, 
with buyers expressing satisfac- 
tion over the additional 
7,000 
releases in the new edition, as 
well as listings of new chart win- 
ners, this year's gold records and 
the listings of favorite "Best Of" 
and 
"Greatest 
Of" 
LP's 
and 
tapes. 
With the holiday season almost 
here, it's more important than 
ever to specify UPS delivery to 
be assured of getting your spe- 
cial Christmas orders on time. 
And don't forget that the "Christ. 
mas Gift" service is still going 
strong and there 
is still time 
to get your orders gift wrapped 
and mailed 
to the appropriate 
partly with card enclosed, cour- 
tesy of FIND.

SPECIAL MERIT PICKS 
POP 
FRANK 
ZAPPA AND 
THE 
MOTHERS -Grand 
Wazoo. Reprise MS 2093 
Frank Zappa has never been content to sit 
on his haunches and reap the glory for his 
past innovations. 
Ever treading onward & 
outward he. and his beloved 
Mothers have 
created 
a new myth replete with musical 
accompaniment. "Mediocrates of Pedestrium" 
is surely the fiend of our time, "Cletus 
Awreetus" 
is 
the very personification 
of 
misguided benevolence. Stockhausen's Cage, 
never! Frank Zappa is his own man, the mu- 
sic was his, and now it's ours, do with it as 
you wish. 
McKENDREE 
SPRING -Tracks. 
Decca 
(MCA) 
DL 7-5385 
McKendree Spring has 
been around for 
a 
long time and have never received the rec- 
ognition that many people feel they deserve. 
Perhaps this excellent set will get them some 
of that recognition. 
Fran McKendree con- 
tinues to 
be the leading force here, with 
strong cuts such as "Friends Die Easy II" 
and "Don't Keep Me Waiting," and the elec- 
tric violin work of Michael Dreyfus is ex- 
cellent as usual, especially on "Light Up 
the Skies." A strong LP from a fine group.

BLUES 
MISSISSIPPI 
JOHN 
HURT -Last 
Sessions. 
Vanguard VSD 79327 
Mississippi 
John Hurt was 
a 
blues giant 
for years, but many members of the pop 
audience never heard of him until the advent 
of the U.S. folk boom in the early '60's 
followed closely 
by the British 
invasion. 
Here, alone with his guitar, he 
is brilliant. 
From the opening "Poor Boy, 
Long Ways 
From 
Home," through 
"Boys You're Wel- 
come," "Let the Mermaids Flirt With Me," 
"All Night Long" and "Goodnight Irene," 
he shows his genius. 
He was a master of 
his music and it's a pity he wasn't recog- 
nized sooner.

SHAWN PHILLIPS 
Bitter End, New York 
After four fine, provocative al- 
bums, Shawn Phillips, A&M Rec- 
ords' artist, has built a small but 
devoted 
following. 
Phillips' per- 
formances at the Bitter End, fo- 
* * * * * * * * * 
LITTLE ELMO 
IS HERE! 
The Evening Star shines. Let 
us sip the universal wine of 
understanding 
. 
. 
. and love. 
And let the reality of this exist- 
ence be known. 
Earthlings, you have been in 
the darkness and in your search 
for the light oftentimes you 
have cried out, believing your 
efforts futile. But it is that your 
cries have been heeded by the 
Mighty Masters of this realm 
and it is that supreme rectifica- 
tion is imminent on your planet 
of confusion. 
My name is Goldie to those 
of your strata. And I am here 
in 
all my glorious splendor 
bringing words of wisdom to 
the wise. And the food of life 
to the rich ... and the needy. 
What gifts have I? I come not 
as a seller of material evils, but 
as a giver of lovegoods-free 
for the asking. 
Ah, my friends of this deso- 
late darkness, behold the spec- 
trum of angelic rainbows of 
such astronomical size as to 
make your world invisible in 
proportion. This is yours-if 
you wish to see 
. 
. 
. and oh, 
that glorious sound of celestial 
symphony singing out from the 
heavens! It is yours-if you 
want to hear. 
I bring love. To make you 
whole. To restore your vision 
and your sound. And the keys 
of love are to be found in the 
truths of which I speak .. .

"Goldie On Love 
& Logic"

Who is 
Needom 
Carroll 
Grantham? 
10 
cusing primarily on his solo abili 
ties as guitarist and vocalist, vin- 
dicated both the intensity and lim- 
ited size of that group. 
Phillips' vocal range is indeed 
extraordinary, but, what startles 
on a recording can be simply abra- 
sive within the confines of a small 
club. As the set progressed, he 
warmed up, and his tone and at- 
tack both improved mightily. Still, 
those loftier excursions were occa- 
sionally shrill, helped not in the 
least by the demands that Phillips 
the composer makes on Phillips 
the vocalist. 
Indeed, the man's entire musical 
personality must be characterized 
as ambitious, leaving the s a f e 
boundaries of the conventional pop 
melody and lyric behind. When 
he succeeds, the product is dazzling, 
atmospheric, 
intensely 
personal; 
when he falls short, one is struck 
only by the pretension. 
Phillips still emerges the victor, 
for even his more oblique material 
is offset by his warmth on stage. 
SAM SUTHERLAND 
BREWER AND SHIPLEY 
DANNY COX 
The Boarding House, 
San Francisco, Ca. 
Kama Sutra recording duo 
Brewer and Shipley sing together 
as though they were born for only 
that purpose. Accompanying them- 
selves on acoustic guitar, they are 
backed throughout their set by 
Larry Knight on electric guitar 
and by Billy Barrasini on bass. 
Their repertoire includes original 
compositions ("One Toke Over the 
Line" and "Tarkio Road"), as well 
as songs written by other perform- 
ers (Dylan's "All Along the Watch- 
tower," among others). All are 
rendered in the same polished and 
professional 
manner. 
The 
real 
highlight of any Brewer and Ship- 
ley performance 
is their 
vocal 
harmonies, which have yet to fall 
below the level of the exceptional. 
Sharing co -billing credit 
with 
Brewer and Shipley is Dunhill's 
Danny Cox. In this age of over - 
amplification it is truly refreshing 
to find an artist like Danny Cox. 
Accompanying himself on acoustic 
guitar throughout, Danny Cox is 
one of that all too rare breed of 
musicians who truly enjoys making 
music. He sings his own composi- 
tions, among them "Lady Luck

People are talking about the 
superb efforts of Program Di- 
rector Roland Bynum and the 
disk jockeys at KGFJ-AM, Los 
Angeles, who formed a basket- 
ball team to raise money for the 
schools in the city and surround- 
ing areas. This year not only 
did they have a winning season 
on the hardwood but reportedly 
raised $20,000 for schools. 
Stax's Staple Singers have been 
selected to represent the U.S. at 
the seventh annual MIDEM in 
Cannes, Jan. 21-27. The family 
group will perform at the Palais 
des Festival before an antici- 
pated audience of over 10,000. 
The performance will be taped 
by West German ZDF TV. 
Andy Stroud, President of 
the newly formed Stroud Rec- 
ords, announced this week the 
label's first release is a very 
timely album by Nina Simone, 
his wife. 
The entry entitled 
"Nina Simone Sings Billie Holi- 
day" features Holiday classics 
from the Motown film "The 
Lady Sings The Blues."

More 
Hot 
Rocks 
(big 
hits 
& 
fazed cookies) 
London 2 PS 626/7 
Without a doubt the Stones are the defini- 
tive rock 'n' roll band. The years cannot 
fade, nor time alter the incredible impact 
that 
they have 
had 
(and will have) 
on 
many lives. Every cut 
on this two -record 
set is, 
of course, 
a 
gem containing that 
magic elixer that spells 
foreverness. 
Flex 
your muscles to "Tell He," "Out of Time," 
"No 
Expectations" and "Come On" (their 
first ever single) plus 21 more.

KING HARVEST 
Dancing in the Moonlight 
Perception PLP 36 
In the chronicles of rock history there have 
been legions of what are known as "one hit 
wonders." 
These 
proverbial 
flash 
in 
the 
pans 
produce 
one 
incredible 
single 
and 
that's it, the full extent of their creative 
energies 
being drained. 
King Harvest will 
not go the way of these momentary 
up- 
starts. Their music is joyous, unpretentious 
rock 'n' roll. 
Especially listen to "Lady 
Come on Home," "You and I" and "Roose- 
velt and Ira Lee."

each note

who gave the work its live U.S. debut in 
September, find all the bombastic fire and 
wryly humorous comments characteristic to 
the Russian titan. This is a provocative work 
with some mind -boggling musical quotations 
from Wagnerian opera, earlier Shostakovich 
and even the Rossini "William Tell Over- 
ture" theme used by the "Lone Ranger."

FIND has 
proved 
a successful 
operation for Byron Weiss, order 
of six Record Center outlets in 
the Denver area. Weiss also runs 
leased departments and acts as a 
wholesaler in some cases. 
"FIND 
is 
working out 
well 
from all aspects for us," Weiss 
says. "We use it extensively in 
our wholesale operation, in which 
we act as a one -stop. We also 
use it in all of our retail outlets 
and in our leased departments. 
In our outlets we keep the cata- 
logs out and we fill in the infor- 
mation for the customer. We also 
advertise that we can get special 
orders, and this helps bring out 
a return business." 
Weiss 
also 
feels 
that 
even 
when an order is not filled, the 
customer will return. "He sees 
the name Billboard on the form," 
he says, "and the average con- 
sumer does know what Billboard 
is and has confidence in it as far 
as music is concerned. 
"Our orders are pretty much 
across the board as far as types 
of 
merchandise 
goes. 
The fill 
has been 
excellent as well as 
delivery time. In our six leased 
departments, mainly in the Den- 
ver 
area 
and 
in 
department 
stores, we also use the catalog 
extensively 
and 
it 
has 
been 
working out. 
"The FIND service has been of 
tremendous help in our wholesale 
operation," Weiss adds. "It has 
aided us in maintaining custom- 
ers and it keeps up their con- 
fidence with us." 
Weiss started with FIND only 
several months 
ago, 
and says 
that up until now the service 
has been everything he expected 
it to 
be. 
He says 
he expects 
to keep using it extensively.

JAZZ 
CHARLIE EARLAND-Live At The Lighthouse. 
Prestige 10050 
Earland's on -location taping produced good, 
funky "gooving" music. What you're groov- 
ing to when you hear it is 
a moot point, 
but the hard, dynamics of his organ aug- 
mented with sax, guitar, bass, trombone and 
congas, gives the overall sound a commercial 
depth of field. From the all appealing open- 
ing, "Smiling," the 
band moves 
into 
a 
straight 
ahead 
4/4 
"We've 
Only 
Just 
Begun." "Black Gun" has 
so 
much Latin 
jazz that it could 
be 
played 
on 
Spanish 
stations. Jazz broadcasters should 
have 
a 
happy day with this album for the material 
is bright and snappy and very down to 
the ground. 
ART BLAKEY AND THE JAZZ MESSENGERS - 
Child's Dance. Prestige 10047 
If you like jazz with a taste of Latin spices 
or hard blowing, this LP offers both. "Song 
For A Lonely Lady" features some romping 
Latin 
percussion 
work 
right 
by drummer 
Blakey's side as Buddy Terry's soprano sax 
spurts along and builds a 
nice 
bridge for 
John Hick's electric piano to follow. This 
is a total group effort, not a seismographic 
demonstration of Blakey's prowess; he fits 
in perfectly as the propellant for such works 
as "C.C." which showcases 
Woody Shaw's 
clear trumpet; "Child's Dance" and "I Can't 
Get Started," the latter slow 
and richly 
rewarding.

JIMMY FORREST-Black Forrest. Delmark 427 
Pretty music is what tenorman Forrest re- 
corded several years ago and which finally 
emerges on this LP. Delmark doesn't actually 
state how old these takes are, but there 
are nine cuts in the work of varying lengths 
and the lyric, melodic beauty of Forrest's 
horn sets 
a happy mood for such sidemen as 
guitarist Grant Green, pianist Harold Mabern 
and 
drummer 
Elvin 
Jones -all 
of 
whom 
are much more in the forefront of 
jazz to- 
day. The sound is mainstream, the format 
standard solo after solo 
ensemble return. 
Green's 
guitar 
is 
especially 
strong. 
The 
title tune is 
a fast, 
no nonsense blowing 
exercise and is a good contrast to the slow, 
romantic 
and 
very brief 
(1:50) "What's 
New?"

is rather

are fun to rehear.

VARIOUS ARTISTS -Roots Of Black Music In 
America. Folkways Records FA 2694 
On -location tapings of drum styles in Africa, 
gospel shouts and cries and what are called 
"some examples" of American black music, 
comprise this two -disk set which has more 
historical value than entertainment impact. 
No artists are credited in Samuel Charters' 
compilation of styles, with the 
last side 
offering blues and jazz examples the most 
interesting. The wide scope of the material 
is its strongest library value.
